title: Codebase and task skills with evals

story: The bug fixer is a routine: the same agent as Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, but started by a triaged bug ticket instead of an assignment. Its first ticket is RH-1240: the dataset API returns an error 500 when a dataset name contains an emoji. The bug is in a Django serializer, the code that turns database rows into API responses.

In the first version of our skills, every description began with "Use when working in fcp". So the fixer loaded the frontend codebase skill too, and spent its first minutes reading about Storybook stories and screen widths for a backend fix. The fix-bug skill, the one that says to reproduce the bug with a failing test before touching the code, never loaded, because its description talked about "triage" and never said the word bug. The fixer changed the line it guessed, and nothing proved the bug was gone.
hook.question: How do we make the right skills load for each task, and only those, and prove it before every machine gets them?

p: Our shared skills come in two kinds. A codebase skill is a map of one area: where things live, the patterns the team uses, and the risky places. fe-codebase covers fcp's frontend, be-codebase the backend modules, devops-codebase the infrastructure and deployment repositories. A task skill is a method for one kind of work, whatever the area: fix-bug, fix-ci, fix-flaky-test, upgrade-dependency, add-tests and a few more. fix-bug, for example, says to reproduce the bug first, at the level the user sees it, then name the root cause with file and line, make the smallest fix, and add the reproduction as a regression test.

A real task usually needs one of each, plus verify. RH-1240 needs be-codebase (where serializers live and why the published SDK must keep working) and fix-bug (reproduce first). It does not need fe-codebase or remove-dead-code. Each wrong skill that loads costs context for the rest of the session and, worse, steers the agent with instructions written for another job.

read.h: Give each kind its own lane
p: The two kinds are told apart in different ways. A codebase skill is about files, so it gets a paths field in its frontmatter: glob patterns such as frontend/**. With paths set, Claude Code offers the skill to Claude automatically only once the session works with a file that matches, for example after it reads or edits frontend/src/components/app/ProjectsTable/ProjectsTable.tsx. A backend fix that never opens a frontend file never sees fe-codebase.

A task skill is about the request, not the files, so its lane is its description: the words people really use for that kind of work. fix-bug's description starts with "Use when the task is a reported bug" and its when_to_use lists "this is broken" and "X shows the wrong value". The description should not claim a whole repository, because then it matches everything.

A codebase skill also stays short. be-codebase is an entry point: it says what matters in the backend and which deeper guide to read for each module (be-module-cloud, be-module-client, be-module-sdk). Those deeper guides load only when the task reaches that module, instead of every backend fix paying for all three.

code.file: the frontmatter of the three codebase skills
code.text:
---
name: fe-codebase
description: "Use when working in fcp/frontend: where things live, the design system, useQuery, layouts from 760 to 1440 px, stories per state, e2e page objects."
paths: ["frontend/**"]
---

---
name: be-codebase
description: "Use when working in fcp cloud, client or sdk: Django and DRF patterns, migrations, the gRPC contract, SDK back-compat."
paths: ["cloud/**", "client/**", "sdk/**", "common/**"]
---

---
name: devops-codebase
description: "Use when working in the infrastructure or gitops repos: Terragrunt trees, modules, Helm and Argo CD, environments."
paths: ["**/terragrunt.hcl", "modules/**", "charts/**"]
---

notes.text: The lane: offered only once the session works with a file under frontend/.
The backend lane covers all four backend folders, including common/ where the gRPC messages live.
Infrastructure lives in other repositories, so the patterns name file types, not one folder.

p: A lane is a claim, so each skill proves it with eval cases, the test cases that claude plugin eval runs with and without the plugin. Every skill needs at least one case where it should fire and change the result, and at least one case where it must stay quiet. Positive cases cannot show a skill that fires too widely, because they only ask the questions it is meant for; only an unrelated request shows it.

The stays-quiet case has one free grader: tool_used on the Skill tool with min 0 and max 0, so the run fails if the skill loads at all. arm: both makes it count in both arms; without it, a Skill grader is only an indicator in a two-arm run. Cases with only free graders like this one are tagged pr and run on every pull request.

A positive case for a codebase skill must give the agent a reason to open a file in its area, because a path-scoped skill is not offered before that. A prompt that only says "plan the empty card" may be answered without opening a file, and then fe-codebase was never even available.

code.text:
schema_version: "1.1"
name: fe-codebase-stays-quiet-on-backend
tags: [pr, fe-codebase]
execution:
  prompt: "Add a last_seen_at field to the Workgroup model in cloud and expose it in the API."
  allowed_tools: [Read, Glob, Grep, Skill]
graders:
  - name: does-not-fire
    type: tool_used
    tool: Skill
    input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?fe-codebase"'
    min: 0
    max: 0
    arm: both

notes.text: A real backend request, written the way a person would type it, with no skill name in it.
Did the Skill tool load fe-codebase? With or without the plugin prefix.
min 0 and max 0: the case passes only when fe-codebase never loads.
Count it in both arms, because staying quiet is the whole point of this case.

deeper.h: Go deeper: cases that need a judge, and the runner's limits
p: Some behaviour cannot be checked with a pattern. be-codebase's case for a protocol change asks whether the answer adds a new field instead of renaming an old one, and says that clients already installed at customers must keep working. That needs an llm grader, a second model that judges the answer against written PASS and FAIL conditions, so the case is tagged nightly and runs once a day with every other judged case instead of on each pull request.

Eval cases set max_turns and timeout_seconds for the eval runner. Our cases raise them well above the tool's defaults, because a good answer that needs many steps should not fail on a turn count. These are settings for one test run, not limits on an agent: in production our agents run with no turn, time or budget limit.

lab.title: Give each skill its lane, then prove it
lab.goal: Give three codebase skills their paths, see which ones each recorded session would be offered, then write the two eval cases that prove fe-codebase fires for its work and stays quiet for the rest.

guess.q: fe-codebase has paths: ["frontend/**"]. Someone asks a question about the projects table, and Claude answers without opening any file. Was fe-codebase offered in that session?

options.text: Yes, because the question is about the frontend
options.why: paths looks at files the session works with, not at the topic of the question.

options.text: No, because no file under frontend/ was touched yet
options.why: A path-scoped skill is offered once the session reads or edits a matching file. Before that, it is not available to load automatically.

options.text: Yes, because every installed skill is always in the list
options.why: Without paths that is true. paths is exactly what limits it.

follow.say: Write four recorded sessions, each with the files it touched, and a small script that applies the paths the way Claude Code does: a skill is offered once the session touches a matching file.
Run it, and look at the last line: a question answered before any file is read gets no codebase skill at all. Remember that when you write a positive eval case.
follow.see:

RH-1240 dataset API returns 500      → be-codebase
widen the agents VPC                 → devops-codebase
a question before any file is read   → (no codebase skill)

lab.build: Write the positive case evals/fe-codebase/story-per-state/case.yaml. Its prompt must make the agent open a frontend file (name the file and ask it to read it), then ask how to add the "No projects yet" card and which tests and stories go with it. Give it two free graders: skill-fired (tool_used on Skill with fe-codebase in input_match) and a regex that finds story or stories, ignoring case. Tag it pr. Then add a fifth session to sessions.json that touches only frontend/e2e/pages/ProjectsPage.ts and run node scope.mjs to see that fe-codebase is offered there too.
checks: node scope.mjs offers exactly one codebase skill to each of the first three sessions and none to the fourth.
The stays-quiet case has min 0, max 0 and arm: both on its Skill grader.
Your positive case's prompt names a file under frontend/, so fe-codebase can be offered at all.
Your fifth session (an e2e page object) is offered fe-codebase.

solution.text:
schema_version: "1.1"
name: fe-codebase-story-per-state
tags: [pr, fe-codebase]
execution:
  prompt: >
    Read frontend/src/components/app/ProjectsTable/ProjectsTable.tsx and plan how to add a
    "No projects yet" card when the table is empty. Which tests and stories should come with it?
  allowed_tools: [Read, Glob, Grep, Skill]
context:
  add_dirs: [fixture]
graders:
  - name: skill-fired
    type: tool_used
    tool: Skill
    input_match: '"skill"\s*:\s*"(?:[\w-]+:)?fe-codebase"'
  - name: story-per-state
    type: regex
    pattern: "stor(y|ies)"
    flags: i

lab.fix: A teammate who always starts Claude Code inside fcp/frontend wrote fe-codebase's paths as ["src/**"], because that is what they see in their terminal. In an agent machine, and for anyone who starts at the root of fcp, the files are called frontend/src/…. Change the paths to ["src/**"] and run node scope.mjs: RH-1234 now gets (no codebase skill). Put it back, and say which eval case would have caught this in CI.
explain: What is the difference between a codebase skill and a task skill, and which one does RH-1240 need of each?
Why does a codebase skill use paths while a task skill relies on its description?
Why can no number of positive cases show that a skill fires too widely?
lab.done: scope.mjs gives every recorded session the right map, and fe-codebase has one case where it must fire and one where it must stay quiet.

check.q: be-codebase has paths: ["cloud/**", "client/**", "sdk/**", "common/**"]. A session fixes a bug and only edits files in frontend/. What happens with be-codebase?

options.text: It is not offered to Claude automatically, because no matching file was touched
options.why: paths limits automatic loading to sessions that work with matching files.

options.text: It loads anyway, because its description mentions fcp
options.why: With paths set, the description alone does not make it available; a matching file must be touched first.

options.text: It loads at the start of every session in the fcp repository
options.why: That is what happens without paths. paths exists to stop exactly that.

check.q: Every skill must have at least one case where it should stay quiet. Why are positive cases not enough?

options.text: Because positive cases cost more model calls
options.why: Both kinds cost the same. The difference is what they can see.

options.text: Because claude plugin eval refuses a suite without a negative case
options.why: The tool does not require one. Our own rule and our CI's case count do.

options.text: Because positive cases only ask what the skill is for, so a skill that also fires on unrelated work passes all of them
options.why: Only a request outside its lane shows that a skill fires too widely and steers work it was not written for.

check.q: Why is be-codebase a short entry point that sends the agent to be-module-cloud, be-module-client or be-module-sdk, instead of one long skill with everything?

options.text: Because a skill file cannot be longer than 100 lines
options.why: There is no such hard limit. The guide suggests short files for a different reason.

options.text: Because a loaded body stays in context for the rest of the session, so the deep guide for a module should load only when the task reaches it
options.why: A fix in the cloud module then pays for the cloud guide, not for the client and SDK guides too.

options.text: Because the module guides belong to other teams
options.why: They belong to the backend guild, like be-codebase. The split is about context, not ownership.

p: The guilds write the codebase skills in their own plugins: fe-codebase in fe-guild (starting from frontend/AGENTS.md and the reviewer memory of the PR review skill, linking instead of copying), be-codebase in be-guild over the moved be-module-* guides, and devops-codebase and infra-change in devops-guild. infra-change explains the checks that need no cloud keys, where a plan comes from, the blast-radius and rollback notes, and that a person applies: agents never apply, destroy or sync.

The task skills are fix-bug and fix-ci in rhino-core, fix-flaky-test in be-guild, then upgrade-dependency, remove-dead-code, add-tests, merge-duplicates and small-feature from the guilds, and security-fix from DevOps with Security. Each has 3 to 10 eval cases with at least one negative case; the routines load them, and ROUTINE-BENCH re-runs its slices on every change. Each skill's owner is named in catalog.yaml.

tickets.why: be-codebase as the short entry point over the module guides, with the protocol-change case.
The remaining task skills and security-fix, each with a stays-quiet case.

words.plain: A map of one area: where things live, the patterns, the risky places.
A method for one kind of work, such as fixing a bug, whatever the area.
A frontmatter field with glob patterns; the skill is offered automatically only once the session works with a matching file.
An eval case with an unrelated request, which passes only if the skill does not load.

review.q: Name the map and the method a CI fixer needs for a broken frontend unit test, and one skill that should stay quiet.
review.a: fe-codebase (the map) and fix-ci (the method), plus verify. be-codebase or remove-dead-code should stay quiet.

review.q: Write the grader lines of a stays-quiet case from memory.
review.a: type: tool_used, tool: Skill, an input_match on the skill name with an optional plugin prefix, min: 0, max: 0, arm: both.

remember: Give each map its paths and each method its words, and prove both directions: a case where the skill must fire and one where it must stay quiet.
